note: 50 mixed-form items across the chapter's concepts. Difficulty 17 Easy / 17 Medium / 16 Hard.

items.stem: The green pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis is
items.explanation: Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs light energy and makes photosynthesis possible.

options.why: Haemoglobin carries oxygen in blood and has no role in plants.
Melanin is an animal pigment that colours skin and hair.
Carotene is an accessory pigment and is not the main absorber.

items.stem: Most absorption of digested food takes place in the
items.explanation: The small intestine has villi that greatly increase the surface area for absorption.

options.why: The stomach mainly digests protein; little absorption happens there.
The large intestine absorbs water, not digested food.
The oesophagus only carries food to the stomach.

items.stem: The number of chambers in the human heart is
items.explanation: There are two atria and two ventricles, making four chambers in all.

options.why: Two chambers describe a fish heart, not a human one.
Three chambers describe an amphibian heart.
No vertebrate heart has five chambers.

items.stem: The basic filtration unit of the kidney is called the
items.explanation: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, and each filters the blood.

options.why: A neuron is a nerve cell, not a kidney unit.
An alveolus is an air sac in the lung.
A villus is a projection in the small intestine.

items.stem: Exchange of gases in the lungs takes place across the
items.explanation: The alveoli have very thin walls and a rich blood supply, which suits them for gas exchange.

options.why: The trachea only conducts air and has thick cartilage walls.
The bronchi conduct air towards the alveoli.
The diaphragm is a muscle that changes the volume of the chest.

items.stem: The end product of anaerobic respiration in human muscle is
items.explanation: Without enough oxygen, pyruvate is converted to lactic acid, which causes cramp.

options.why: Ethanol is produced by yeast, not by human muscle.
These are the products of aerobic respiration.
Glucose is the starting material, not a product.

items.stem: Double circulation means that blood passes through the heart
items.explanation: Blood goes through the heart twice in one complete circuit, once to the lungs and once to the body.

options.why: A single circulation is found in fishes, not in mammals.
Blood flows in one direction, controlled by valves.
There is one heart, divided into two halves.

items.stem: Water rises to the top of a tall tree chiefly because of
items.explanation: Evaporation from the leaves creates a suction that pulls the continuous column of water upwards through the xylem.

options.why: Root pressure is significant only at night and in short plants.
Xylem vessels are dead tubes and cannot pump.
Capillarity cannot raise water more than a metre or so.

items.stem: Pancreatic juice cannot act in the stomach because
items.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes need an alkaline medium, and the stomach contents are strongly acidic.

options.why: Pancreatic juice is rich in trypsin, lipase and amylase.

options.text: the stomach has no blood supply
options.why: The stomach is well supplied with blood.

options.text: food does not enter the stomach
options.why: Food certainly enters the stomach first.

items.stem: Stomata close when the guard cells
items.explanation: Guard cells lose water, become flaccid and shrink, which closes the pore between them.

options.why: Swelling guard cells open the pore rather than closing it.
Guard cells do not divide to control the pore.
Guard cells keep their chloroplasts throughout.

items.stem: What are life processes?
items.answer: Life processes are the essential activities that maintain and repair the body of a living organism, including nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion. They continue even when the organism is not doing anything visible.

items.stem: How does autotrophic nutrition differ from heterotrophic nutrition?
items.answer: An autotroph makes its own food from simple inorganic substances using an outside energy source, as green plants do using sunlight. A heterotroph cannot do this and must take in food made by other organisms.

items.stem: What are peristaltic movements?
items.answer: They are rhythmic waves of contraction and relaxation of the muscles in the wall of the alimentary canal, which push the food forward along it.

items.stem: Why is ATP called the energy currency of the cell?
items.answer: Energy released during respiration is stored in ATP, and the cell then spends ATP whenever energy is needed for any process. Like currency, it is a common form in which energy is held and transferred.

items.stem: Why do arteries have thick elastic walls while veins have valves?
items.answer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, so their walls must be thick and elastic to withstand and smooth out the surge. Veins carry blood at low pressure, so they need valves to prevent the blood from flowing backwards.

items.stem: Name the two conducting tissues in plants and state what each carries.
items.answer: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals upwards from the roots. Phloem carries the food made in the leaves to all other parts, and can move it in either direction.

items.stem: Why is glucose absent from the urine of a healthy person although it is filtered by the kidney?
items.answer: Glucose is small enough to pass into the filtrate, but it is a useful nutrient, so it is selectively reabsorbed into the blood as the filtrate travels along the tubule. Only when the blood glucose is abnormally high does the reabsorption capacity get exceeded and glucose appear in urine.

items.stem: Why does aerobic respiration release far more energy than anaerobic respiration from the same glucose?
items.answer: Aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing almost all the energy stored in its bonds. Anaerobic respiration stops at lactic acid or ethanol, which still contain a great deal of chemical energy, so most of the available energy is left unreleased.

items.stem: State the raw materials, conditions and products of photosynthesis, and write the equation.
items.answer: The raw materials are carbon dioxide, taken in through the stomata from the air, and water, absorbed by the roots and carried up by the xylem. The conditions required are sunlight, which supplies the energy, and chlorophyll, which absorbs that light and is held in the chloroplasts. The products are glucose, which is stored as starch, and oxygen, which is released through the stomata. The equation is carbon dioxide plus water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, gives glucose plus oxygen. The process is endothermic, absorbing energy from sunlight and storing it in the chemical bonds of the glucose, which is why it is the origin of almost all food on Earth.

items.stem: Trace the path of food through the human alimentary canal, naming what happens at each stage.
items.answer: Food enters the mouth, where teeth break it up and saliva containing amylase begins the digestion of starch. Swallowing passes it to the oesophagus, where peristalsis pushes it down to the stomach. In the stomach, gastric juice supplies hydrochloric acid, which makes the medium acidic and kills bacteria, and pepsin, which digests protein; the churning also mixes the food thoroughly. The partly digested food then enters the small intestine, where bile from the liver makes the medium alkaline and emulsifies fats, and pancreatic juice supplies amylase, trypsin and lipase to complete the digestion of carbohydrate, protein and fat. Absorption of the digested food happens here through the villi. What remains passes to the large intestine, where water is absorbed, and the indigestible residue is stored in the rectum and expelled through the anus.

items.stem: Describe the path of blood through the human heart, naming the chambers and vessels in order.
items.answer: Deoxygenated blood from the body returns through the vena cava into the right atrium. The right atrium contracts and pushes it through a valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle contracts and pumps it through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it loses carbon dioxide and takes up oxygen. The oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium. The left atrium contracts and pushes it into the left ventricle. The left ventricle, which has the thickest wall of all four chambers, contracts powerfully and pumps the blood through the aorta to the whole body. Valves between the atria and ventricles, and at the exits of the ventricles, ensure the blood moves in one direction only. Because the blood passes through the heart twice in one full circuit, once for the lungs and once for the body, the arrangement is called double circulation.

items.stem: Explain how the human lungs are adapted to maximise the exchange of gases.
items.answer: Four adaptations work together. First, the bronchi branch repeatedly into finer bronchioles ending in millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli, so the total surface area available for exchange is enormous, of the order of a tennis court in a space the size of the chest. Second, the alveolar wall is only one cell thick, so the distance a gas must diffuse between air and blood is as short as possible. Third, each alveolus is wrapped in a dense network of capillaries, so blood is always close by and the concentration difference that drives diffusion is maintained. Fourth, the alveolar surface is kept moist, which is necessary because gases must dissolve before they can diffuse across a membrane. Ventilation by the ribs and diaphragm continually replaces the air, keeping the oxygen concentration in the alveoli high and the carbon dioxide concentration low.

items.stem: Describe three types of heterotrophic nutrition with an example of each.
items.answer: Saprophytic nutrition, in which the organism secretes enzymes onto dead and decaying matter outside its body and absorbs the digested products. Fungi such as bread mould and mushrooms feed this way, and they are important as decomposers. Parasitic nutrition, in which the organism lives on or inside another living organism and takes its nourishment from it, usually harming the host. Cuscuta on a plant, and tapeworm and Plasmodium in animals, are examples. Holozoic nutrition, in which the organism takes in solid or liquid food, digests it inside the body and then absorbs it. Amoeba does this by engulfing a food particle, and human beings do it through the alimentary canal. The three differ in whether digestion happens outside the body, inside a host, or inside the organism's own digestive system.

items.stem: Why is double circulation necessary in birds and mammals but not in fishes?
items.answer: Birds and mammals are warm-blooded and must generate heat continuously to keep their body temperature constant, which requires a very high rate of respiration and therefore a rapid and efficient supply of oxygen. Double circulation serves this by keeping the oxygenated and deoxygenated blood completely separate through a four-chambered heart. Blood going to the body is fully oxygenated, and it is pumped at high pressure by the thick-walled left ventricle, so it reaches the tissues quickly. Passing through the heart a second time restores the pressure lost in the lungs, which would otherwise leave the body circulation sluggish. A fish is cold-blooded and does not need to generate heat, so its oxygen demand is much lower. Its two-chambered heart pumps blood once to the gills and then straight on to the body, and although the pressure falls, the slower supply is sufficient. So the difference in circulation follows from the difference in energy requirement.

items.stem: Explain how water reaches the top of a tall tree, and state two other uses of transpiration.
items.answer: Water is absorbed by the root hairs and passes into the xylem, which forms continuous open tubes from the root to every leaf. At the leaf, water evaporates from the surface of the cells and diffuses out through the stomata. This loss creates a shortage in the leaf cells, which draw water from the xylem, and because water molecules attract one another strongly the whole column is pulled up as a single thread. This suction, called transpiration pull, is powerful enough to raise water many metres, far beyond what capillarity or root pressure could achieve. Root pressure contributes mainly at night when transpiration has stopped. Transpiration has two further uses. It cools the plant, since evaporation takes heat from the leaf, which is important in strong sunlight. It also carries dissolved minerals absorbed by the roots upwards to wherever they are needed, so the same stream that supplies water distributes nutrition.

items.stem: Explain why the medium changes from acidic in the stomach to alkaline in the small intestine.
items.answer: Each set of enzymes works best over a narrow range of pH, and the digestive tract is organised so that each gets its own conditions. In the stomach, gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid, which makes the contents strongly acidic at about pH 2. This is necessary because pepsin, the protein-digesting enzyme there, is active only in acid, and the acid also kills most bacteria swallowed with the food. When the partly digested food passes into the small intestine, that acidity would destroy the enzymes waiting there, since pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase all need an alkaline medium. Bile from the liver, which is alkaline, neutralises the acid and shifts the pH upwards, and pancreatic juice is itself alkaline. Bile performs a second task at the same time, breaking large fat globules into small droplets so that lipase has a much greater surface to work on. The arrangement shows a general principle: the body does not use one universal set of conditions but creates a sequence of environments, each suited to the stage of digestion occurring in it.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Green plants can make their own food. Reason (R): They contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and chlorophyll capturing light is exactly what makes autotrophic nutrition possible.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Capturing light energy is precisely what allows food to be made.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Green plants genuinely contain chlorophyll.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Green plants are autotrophs and do make their own food.

items.stem: Assertion (A): The alveolar wall is one cell thick. Reason (R): This shortens the diffusion distance for gases. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and a shorter diffusion path is exactly why the thin wall is an advantage.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: The short diffusion path is precisely the benefit of thinness.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A shorter path genuinely speeds diffusion.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: The alveolar wall really is a single cell thick.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Anaerobic respiration is more efficient than aerobic respiration. Reason (R): Anaerobic respiration does not require oxygen. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: not needing oxygen is an advantage in supply, not in energy yield, and the yield is far lower.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Avoiding the need for oxygen does not increase the energy released.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Anaerobic respiration genuinely proceeds without oxygen.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Incomplete breakdown leaves most of the energy in the product.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Urine is simply the filtrate produced by the glomerulus. Reason (R): The glomerulus filters the blood under pressure. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: most of the filtrate, including glucose and much water, is reabsorbed before urine is formed.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Selective reabsorption changes the filtrate greatly before it becomes urine.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Filtration under pressure at the glomerulus genuinely occurs.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: About 99 per cent of the filtered water is reabsorbed.

items.stem: State whether true or false: oxygen is a product of photosynthesis.
items.explanation: Oxygen is released through the stomata as a product of photosynthesis.

options.why: Photosynthesis produces glucose and releases oxygen.

items.stem: State whether true or false: all arteries carry oxygenated blood.
items.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs, so the rule is about direction, not oxygen.

options.why: The pulmonary artery is an exception; arteries are defined by carrying blood away from the heart.

items.stem: State whether true or false: stomata usually close at night.
items.explanation: With no photosynthesis at night there is no need to take in carbon dioxide, so closing the stomata saves water.

options.why: Closing at night conserves water when carbon dioxide is not needed.

items.stem: State whether true or false: phloem transport requires energy while xylem transport does not.
items.explanation: Translocation in the phloem uses ATP to load sugars, whereas xylem transport is driven by evaporation and needs no energy from the plant.

options.why: Phloem loading is an active process using ATP; xylem flow is driven by transpiration pull.

items.stem: The tiny pores on a leaf through which gases are exchanged are called ___________.
items.answer: stomata

items.stem: The chamber of the heart with the thickest muscular wall is the ___________.
items.answer: left ventricle

items.stem: The enzyme present in saliva that digests starch is ___________.
items.answer: amylase

items.stem: The artificial process used to filter the blood when the kidneys fail is called ___________.
items.answer: dialysis

items.stem: Explain what is meant by life processes and why each of nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion is essential.
items.answer: Life processes are the activities that maintain and repair the body of a living organism and keep it alive. They continue whether or not the organism is visibly active, which is why a sleeping animal and a still plant are both alive. Nutrition is essential because the body needs an outside source of energy and of the materials from which it is built and repaired. An autotroph makes its food from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight, while a heterotroph must take in food made by others. Respiration is essential because the energy held in food is locked in chemical bonds and must be released in a controlled way before it can be used; respiration transfers it into ATP, which the cell can spend. Transport is essential because in any organism larger than a few cells, diffusion alone is far too slow to carry food and oxygen to every cell and carry wastes away, so a circulatory system in animals and xylem and phloem in plants are needed. Excretion is essential because the chemical reactions of the body produce wastes such as urea and carbon dioxide which are poisonous if they accumulate, so they must be removed continuously. The four are interdependent: transport carries what nutrition supplies, respiration uses it, and excretion removes what respiration leaves behind.

items.stem: Describe the human circulatory system, naming its parts and explaining the function of each.
items.answer: The system consists of the heart, the blood vessels and the blood. The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump with two atria above and two ventricles below. The atria receive blood returning to the heart and the ventricles pump it out, and the left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must drive blood round the whole body. Valves between the atria and ventricles and at the exits of the ventricles prevent backflow. There are three kinds of vessel. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure and so have thick elastic walls and narrow openings. Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure, so they have thinner walls, wider openings and valves to stop the blood falling back. Capillaries are one cell thick and form fine networks in the tissues, which is where the actual exchange of materials happens. The blood consists of plasma, which carries dissolved food, carbon dioxide, urea and hormones; red blood cells, which contain haemoglobin and carry oxygen; white blood cells, which fight infection; and platelets, which help the blood to clot. A separate lymphatic system collects fluid that has leaked from the capillaries and returns it to the blood, also carrying absorbed fat from the intestine.

items.stem: Describe the events of photosynthesis in sequence and explain how each raw material reaches the chloroplast.
items.answer: Photosynthesis happens in three stages. First, the chlorophyll in the chloroplast absorbs light energy. Second, that energy splits water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen, and the oxygen is released as a by-product. Third, the hydrogen is used to reduce carbon dioxide to carbohydrate, and the light energy absorbed in the first stage is now stored in the chemical bonds of the glucose formed. The three stages need not occur together in time, which is why some plants fix carbon dioxide at night and complete the process by day. Each raw material reaches the chloroplast by its own route. Carbon dioxide diffuses in from the air through the stomata, which are pores on the leaf surface guarded by guard cells that open and close them; the gas then diffuses through the air spaces between the leaf cells and into the chloroplasts. Water is absorbed from the soil by the root hairs, passes into the xylem and is drawn up the stem to the leaf by transpiration pull, then moves into the cells. Sunlight falls directly on the leaf, whose broad flat shape and thin cross-section are adaptations to absorb as much as possible and to let it reach the chloroplasts, which are concentrated in the upper layers. Minerals such as nitrogen and magnesium, needed to build chlorophyll and proteins, are absorbed with the water from the soil. The glucose produced is either used at once in respiration, converted to starch and stored, or carried away in the phloem to other parts of the plant.

items.stem: Explain how urine is formed in the kidney, and evaluate why dialysis cannot fully replace a working kidney.
items.answer: Urine formation has three stages. Filtration occurs at the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule, where blood arrives under pressure and water, glucose, salts, amino acids and urea are forced out into the tubule, while blood cells and large proteins are held back. Selective reabsorption occurs along the tubule, where substances the body needs are taken back into the surrounding blood capillaries: all the glucose, most of the salts and amino acids, and about ninety-nine per cent of the water. Secretion adds a few further wastes directly into the tubule. What remains is urine, which collects in the collecting duct, passes down the ureter to the urinary bladder, is stored there, and is expelled through the urethra. The amount of water reabsorbed is adjusted according to how much the body has available, which is why urine is concentrated when one has drunk little. Dialysis reproduces only the first part of this. Blood is passed through tubes of a selectively permeable membrane immersed in a dialysing fluid that contains the same concentration of glucose and salts as healthy plasma but no urea, so wastes diffuse out while useful substances do not. What it cannot reproduce is the fine, continuous regulation a kidney performs. A kidney monitors the body's state moment by moment and adjusts water and salt reabsorption accordingly, whereas dialysis happens intermittently for a few hours at a time, so between sessions wastes accumulate and the water balance drifts. A kidney also has hormonal functions, helping to control blood pressure and to stimulate the making of red blood cells, which a dialysis machine does not perform at all. Dialysis therefore keeps a patient alive and is invaluable, but it is a partial substitute for an organ, which is why transplantation remains the better outcome where it is possible.

items.stem: If a human heart beats 72 times a minute, how many times does it beat in one hour?
items.answer: Multiply the rate by the number of minutes: 72 times 60, which is 4320 beats in one hour. Over a day this becomes 4320 times 24, that is 103680 beats, which shows how continuously the heart works.

items.stem: A person breathes 16 times a minute, taking in 500 mL of air each time. Find the volume of air breathed in one hour.
items.answer: Air breathed in one minute is 16 times 500 mL, which is 8000 mL, that is 8 litres. In one hour this is 8 times 60, which is 480 litres. Note that only part of each breath reaches the alveoli, since some fills the trachea and bronchi where no exchange occurs, so the volume actually used for gas exchange is less than this figure.

items.stem: About 180 litres of filtrate are produced daily by the kidneys, yet only 1.8 litres of urine are passed. Find the percentage of water reabsorbed and comment.
items.answer: Water reabsorbed is 180 litres minus 1.8 litres, which is 178.2 litres. As a percentage of the filtrate this is 178.2 divided by 180, times 100, which is 99 per cent. So only one per cent of the filtered volume leaves the body. The comment worth making is that this is why filtration alone would be fatal: losing 180 litres of water a day is impossible, and the kidney's essential work is not the filtering but the selective reabsorption that follows it. It also explains why the volume of urine varies so much with how much one drinks, since the reabsorbed fraction is adjusted rather than fixed.

items.stem: Match each enzyme in Column I with what it digests in Column II. Column I: (a) amylase, (b) pepsin, (c) lipase, (d) trypsin. Column II: (i) protein in the stomach, (ii) fat, (iii) starch, (iv) protein in the small intestine.
items.answer: (a) amylase - (iii) starch. (b) pepsin - (i) protein in the stomach, working in acid. (c) lipase - (ii) fat, after bile has emulsified it. (d) trypsin - (iv) protein in the small intestine, working in alkali.

items.stem: Match each structure in Column I with its function in Column II. Column I: (a) red blood cell, (b) platelet, (c) capillary, (d) vein valve. Column II: (i) prevents backflow of blood, (ii) site of exchange with tissues, (iii) carries oxygen, (iv) helps blood to clot.
items.answer: (a) red blood cell - (iii) carries oxygen, using haemoglobin. (b) platelet - (iv) helps blood to clot. (c) capillary - (ii) site of exchange with the tissues. (d) vein valve - (i) prevents backflow of blood.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of the human digestive system and mark where each type of digestion occurs.
items.answer: Draw the alimentary canal as a continuous tube and label, in order, the mouth with teeth and salivary glands, the oesophagus, the stomach, the small intestine with its coils, the large intestine, the rectum and the anus. Draw the liver above and to the right of the stomach with the gall bladder beneath it, and the pancreas below and behind the stomach, and show ducts from both leading into the beginning of the small intestine. Now annotate where each digestion occurs. At the mouth, mark salivary amylase beginning starch digestion. At the stomach, mark hydrochloric acid and pepsin digesting protein in an acidic medium, and note the churning. At the start of the small intestine, mark bile from the liver making the medium alkaline and emulsifying fat, and pancreatic juice supplying amylase, trypsin and lipase to complete the digestion of all three food types. Along the small intestine, mark the villi and label them as the site of absorption of digested food. At the large intestine, mark absorption of water. At the rectum, mark storage of undigested residue. Add a note that the alkaline medium is created before the pancreatic enzymes act, because they cannot work in acid.

items.stem: Draw and label the human respiratory system, and annotate the diagram with the adaptations for gas exchange.
items.answer: Draw the nostrils leading to the nasal passage, then the pharynx, the larynx and the trachea with rings of cartilage shown in its wall. Show the trachea dividing into two bronchi, one to each lung, and each bronchus branching repeatedly into finer bronchioles ending in clusters of small sacs. Enlarge one cluster in an inset and label the individual sacs as alveoli, drawing a network of capillaries wrapped around them. Label the ribs, the intercostal muscles between them, and the dome-shaped diaphragm below the lungs. Now annotate the adaptations. Against the alveoli, note that there are millions of them, giving an enormous total surface area. Against the alveolar wall, note that it is one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is minimal. Against the capillary network, note the rich blood supply, which maintains the concentration difference that drives diffusion. Against the alveolar lining, note that it is kept moist, since gases must dissolve before diffusing. Against the rings of cartilage in the trachea, note that they keep the airway open at all times. Against the diaphragm and ribs, note that their movement changes the volume of the chest and so draws air in and forces it out, continually refreshing the air in the alveoli. Add a final note that the nasal passage warms, moistens and filters the incoming air.

items.stem: Describe an experiment to prove that carbon dioxide is necessary for photosynthesis.
items.answer: Take a healthy potted plant and destarch it by keeping it in complete darkness for two to three days, so that any starch already present is used up; test one leaf with iodine to confirm that no blue-black colour appears. Now take two similar leaves still attached to the plant. Enclose the first in a conical flask containing a little potassium hydroxide solution, held so that the solution does not touch the leaf, and seal the mouth of the flask around the petiole with split cork and grease. Enclose the second leaf in an identical flask containing only water, sealed in the same way. Place the whole plant in sunlight for several hours. Then detach both leaves, boil each in water, then in alcohol to remove the chlorophyll, wash it and test it with iodine solution. The leaf from the flask containing water turns blue-black, showing that starch has been made and therefore that photosynthesis has occurred. The leaf from the flask containing potassium hydroxide does not turn blue-black, showing that no starch was made. The reasoning is as follows. Potassium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide, so the air around the first leaf was free of it, while the second leaf had normal air. Everything else was identical for the two leaves: the same plant, the same sunlight, the same water supply, the same temperature and the same enclosure in a flask. The only difference was the presence of carbon dioxide. Since starch formed only where carbon dioxide was available, carbon dioxide is necessary for photosynthesis. The destarching step is essential to the proof, because without it the blue-black colour might come from starch made before the experiment began, and the second flask is essential as a control, because without it the failure of the first leaf could be blamed on being enclosed rather than on the absence of carbon dioxide.
